clinicalPearls: A contiguous gene deletion of chromosome 11p11.2 producing a combination of skeletal, cranial, and neurodevelopmental features
Multiple cartilaginous exostoses arise from deletion of EXT2, the same gene implicated in hereditary multiple exostoses
Enlarged parietal foramina, defects of membranous skull ossification, result from loss of ALX4
Intellectual disability and developmental delay are usual and reflect deletion of additional genes in the interval
Craniofacial features may include brachycephaly, a broad forehead, and midface differences
The size of the deletion correlates broadly with the range of features, as a larger interval removes more contiguous genes
Exostoses carry a small lifelong risk of malignant transformation and merit orthopaedic surveillance
Diagnosis is by chromosomal microarray defining the extent of the 11p11.2 deletion
reference.pathophysiology: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion disorder in which loss of a segment of chromosome 11p11.2 removes several dosage-sensitive genes together. Haploinsufficiency of EXT2 impairs heparan sulfate biosynthesis in the growth plate and underlies the multiple exostoses, while loss of ALX4 disrupts the ossification of the cranial vault and produces enlarged parietal foramina. Deletion of further genes within the interval contributes to intellectual disability and the craniofacial phenotype. Because the manifestations arise from the combined effect of adjacent genes, the breadth and severity of the picture depend on which genes the individual deletion encompasses.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary multiple exostoses from an isolated EXT2 or EXT1 variant
Isolated enlarged parietal foramina from an ALX4 or MSX2 variant
Other contiguous gene deletion syndromes detected on microarray
Non-specific intellectual disability of alternative genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to confirm the 11p11.2 deletion and delineate its boundaries
Skeletal survey to document exostoses and their distribution
Skull imaging to characterise parietal foramina and ossification defects
Orthopaedic review with ongoing surveillance of exostoses
Parental testing and genetic counselling regarding recurrence risk
redFlags: Rapid growth, pain, or change in an exostosis suggesting malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma
Neurological compromise from an exostosis impinging on nerves or the spinal cord
Large parietal skull defect leaving the underlying brain vulnerable to injury
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is generally normal, and the outlook depends on the degree of intellectual disability and the burden of skeletal disease; exostoses may require surgical treatment and carry a small but real risk of malignant change, so lifelong orthopaedic surveillance is advised, while cranial ossification defects are usually of cosmetic and protective rather than functional concern.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated hereditary multiple exostoses and missing the wider contiguous deletion syndrome
Failing to arrange orthopaedic surveillance for malignant transformation of exostoses
Overlooking the protective implications of large parietal skull defects
Using low-resolution cytogenetics that cannot reliably size the deletion
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy exists; care is directed at the skeletal, cranial and neurodevelopmental manifestations
Orthopaedic surveillance of multiple exostoses with surgical excision of lesions causing pain, deformity, nerve or vessel compression, or restricted movement
Long-term monitoring of exostoses for malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma
Protection and, where required, surgical or supportive management of enlarged parietal foramina and cranial ossification defects
Early developmental intervention and individualised educational support for intellectual disability and developmental delay
Multidisciplinary follow-up spanning clinical genetics, orthopaedics, neurology and developmental paediatrics
Genetic counselling with parental testing to establish recurrence risk
